newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels step up fight against former allies.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels step up fight against former allies.

text.p: Zairean rebels ordered on Tuesday the arrest of leaders of the Mai-Mai village warriors who until last months were their allies in the fight to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Star Radio, the mouthpiece of the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Libertation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), said the decision had been taken because of the trouble the Mai-Mai had caused in one of their home regions north of Goma -- one of several towns in eastern Zaire held by the rebels.
"What the troublemakers are doing is not acceptable and must be stopped," the radio said.

At least 33 people, including 20 Mai-Mai, have been killed in the past week as warriors emerged from their villages in forested hills to attack alliance soldiers at Butembo, 180 km (110 miles) north of Goma.
No casualty figures are known from other outbreaks of fighting near Rwindi 100 km (60 miles) north of Goma and around Bunia, in a gold mining region 360 km (220 miles) to the north.

In little over three months the ADFL, led by longtime Mobutu opponent Laurent Kabila, has taken over a strip of territory more than 600 km (400 miles) long against Zaire's eastern border with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.

The rebels were intitially composed mostly of Rwandan-trained Banyamulenge, an ethnic Tutsi group, but other groups like the Mai-Mai and Ngilima warriors volunteered to join the battle against Zaire's ragged army.

But the new conflict between the rebel factions themselves has called into question the strength of the alliance between the disciplined Banyamulenge and other local ethnic groups in the face of a possible counter-attack by government troops.

"The Banyamulenge and the Mai-Mai both said they had joined together to liberate us and now they are fighting each other. Obviously we have to ask what are the real motives of either group, because somebody must be lying," said student Kakule Kitumbo.

Although thousands of young men have been recruited into the alliance and sent for training at the Rumangabo military camp 60 km (40 miles) north of Goma, they have yet to join the fighting and the core of alliance troops remains the ethnic Tutsis.
Kabila last month ordered the Mai-Mai disarmed after reports of violence against local people. Some of the Mai-Mai accepted the offer of military training in exchange for their weapons.

The Mai-Mai, who believe magic fetishes make them both invisible in battle and invulnerable to bullets, are mostly teenage village recruits who have taken up a tradition of fighting to defend their land.
Last month Kabila said the rebels had beaten back several counter-attacks by government troops. Mobutu has promised to do all in his power to drive the rebels out of Zaire.
It is unclear how far the fighters have been able to advance towards their proclaimed target -- Zaire's fourth largest city of Kisangani, 600 km (400 miles) deep into the forest.

"We are pretty sure the alliance has taken Walikale, but that is still only 130 km (80 miles) from Goma, and it seems the Zaire army is still in control of Lubutu," said one Western aid worker. Lubutu is about halfway between Walikale and Kisangani.
Africa's latest war was ignited by Zairean attempts to expel the Banyamulenge back to Rwanda, a land they left up to 200 years ago.
